The dundun is a West African hourglass-shaped membranophone, also called the talking drum, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.242.11. Its two heads are joined by leather tension cords; the player holds the drum between the armpit and the ribs and squeezes or releases the cords with the arm to change the pitch, imitating the tones and rhythms of human speech. The drum is common in the music of hereditary musicians (griots), and is also used in ritual, weddings, funerals, private occasions and African bands; in some West African societies it can also carry messages through pitch and rhythm.
敦敦鼓為西非沙漏形膜鳴鼓，演奏時將鼓身夾於腋下與肋骨之間，以手臂擠壓皮繩改變鼓面: The dundun is a West African hourglass-shaped membranophone. Hold the body between the armpit and the ribs while playing and squeeze the leather cords with the arm to change the tension of the head; released, the pitch is lower, pressed, it rises, and the pitch can change within a single stroke. Beginners should first practise holding the drum steadily and controlling the amount of squeeze, then imitate speech tones with different pitches and rhythms. When learning drum speech, remember the fixed short phrase that each word matches, and use the surrounding context to reduce ambiguity; do not substitute freely.
敦敦鼓音色低沉厚重，具有溫潤而深邃的音響特徵。其音域位於打擊樂器的低頻範圍，能夠: The dundun's timbre is deep and heavy, warm and profound. Its range lies in the low frequencies of percussion, producing long, resonant low vibration that gives the band a firm rhythmic foundation. The resonance of the vibrating head is distinctive: the sound waves circulate fully in the cavity, which makes the tone full and powerful. Beside bright, high-pitched drums the dundun is steadier and more inward; beside the bass it has more human warmth and folk character. In West African bands the dundun is often interwoven with other percussion, its low resonance in dialogue with the high drums, together building a layered rhythmic fabric and a distinctive African musical flavour.
敦敦鼓鼓身採用實心木桶製造，多使用非洲硬木如紅木或柚木。鼓面為天然動物皮革，通常: The body of the dundun is made from a solid wooden barrel, usually African hardwood such as mahogany or teak. The head is natural animal skin, usually cowhide or goatskin, traditionally treated and tensioned. The rim is reinforced with wood or a metal ring. The striking tools are wooden sticks and the hands; the sticks are usually of hardwood with the tips wrapped in leather or cloth to adjust the timbre. In traditional making metal fittings such as iron rings strengthen the body and the sound.
沙漏形敦敦鼓被視為西非格里奧最古老樂器之一，可追溯至波諾、約魯巴、迦納帝國與豪薩: The hourglass-shaped dundun is regarded as one of the oldest instruments of the West African griots and can be traced back to Bono, Yoruba, the Ghana empire and Hausa. By the eighteenth century drummers were already sending messages of ritual and command by pitch, over four to five miles, relayed by other drummers up to twenty miles. The Yoruba and Dagomba developed griot music centred on the dundun; the Serer tama is used for coming-of-age rites and royal occasions. In the twentieth century the dundun entered West African popular music such as mbalax in Senegal, and fuji and jùjú in Nigeria, and it is also used at weddings, funerals and in band line-ups.
